nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the imperial adventure romance and the lost-world story
literary_identity: Novelist and agricultural reformer; the author of King Solomon's Mines and She, and the founder of the modern adventure romance of Africa.
biography: Born Henry Rider Haggard at Bradenham, Norfolk, on 22 June 1856; he went to South Africa in 1875 as secretary to the governor of Natal and served on the staff of Sir Theophilus Shepstone during the annexation of the Transvaal, returning to England in 1879. King Solomon's Mines (1885) made him famous at once, and he published over sixty books, including She (1887), Allan Quatermain (1887), Cleopatra (1889) and Eric Brighteyes (1891). He served on agricultural commissions in the 1890s and was knighted in 1912, dying in London on 14 May 1925.
literary_profile: Haggard wrote the adventure romance of the imperial world: his Africa is a place of lost civilisations, ancient treasure and supernatural women, and his narrative method — the plain testimony of the hunter, the discovered document, the framing editor — gave the fantastic a documentary authority that the modern adventure story has never lost. He was also a serious critic of the imperial project in his own way, and Ayesha is one of the great disturbing figures of English fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: The first-person testimony of the practical man; the frame narrative and the discovered manuscript; the precise geographical and ethnographic detail; the ordeal and the escape; the archaic and the supernatural encountered as fact.
intellectual_concerns: Empire and the exploration of Africa; the lost civilisation and the ancient world; the supernatural woman and the limits of knowledge; courage, hunting and masculine virtue; reincarnation and immortality; race and the imperial imagination.
historical_significance: Haggard founded the modern adventure romance and the lost-world story: King Solomon's Mines and She created the formula of the imperial adventure that Conan Doyle, Kipling and the cinema would develop, and Ayesha is one of the most influential female figures in English popular fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the naturalist novel, the memoir and the literature of the 1890s
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and autobiographer; the Irish writer who brought French naturalism into English fiction and the first great modern Irish prose writer.
biography: Born George Augustus Moore at Ballyglass, County Mayo, on 24 February 1852, the son of a landowner and MP; he went to Paris in 1873 to study painting, met Manet, Zola and the Impressionists, and returned to London in 1880. A Modern Lover (1883), A Mummer's Wife (1885) and Esther Waters (1894) brought French naturalism into English; he helped found the Irish Literary Theatre in 1899 and wrote the memoir Hail and Farewell (1911-14). He died in London on 21 January 1933.
literary_profile: Moore wrote the English naturalist novel and the modern literary memoir: A Mummer's Wife and Esther Waters treat the lives of the working woman and the servant with a frankness about sex, money and drink that no English novelist had attempted, and Esther Waters is the finest English novel of domestic service. His later Irish books, The Untilled Field and Hail and Farewell, invented the modern Irish short story and the irreverent literary memoir.
stylistic_characteristics: Flaubertian impersonality and exact detail; the plain record of work, wages and drink; the unsparing treatment of sexuality; the free indirect style; the colloquial Irish speech of the later stories; the anecdotal and malicious memoir.
intellectual_concerns: The working woman and domestic service; poverty, drink and the London streets; the Irish land and the Irish peasant; the artist and the literary world; religion and the Catholic childhood; the machinery of literary reputation.
historical_significance: Moore is the founder of English naturalism and the first modern Irish prose writer: Esther Waters is the classic English novel of the servant and one of the great novels of the 1890s, The Untilled Field made the modern Irish short story possible, and Hail and Farewell is the most entertaining literary memoir in the language.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English-Jewish; the ghetto novel, the problem play and the literature of immigration
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and Zionist; the first English writer to make the Jewish immigrant experience the subject of major fiction.
biography: Born in London on 21 February 1864, the son of Russian-Polish Jewish immigrants; he was educated at the Jews' Free School and at London University, became a teacher and then a journalist, and published The Children of the Ghetto in 1892, which made him famous as the 'Dickens of the Ghetto'. He wrote the play The Melting Pot (1908), was an early Zionist and later a territorialist, and campaigned for women's suffrage. He died at Midhurst, Sussex, on 1 August 1926.
literary_profile: Zangwill wrote the English novel of the immigrant: The Children of the Ghetto and its sequels are the first substantial English fiction about the Jewish East End, and they record the speech, the poverty, the religion and the humour of the immigrant community with exactness and affection. He was also the first English writer to make the ghetto the subject of serious literature, and The Melting Pot gave the language its phrase for the American assimilation of immigrants.
stylistic_characteristics: Dialect speech transcribed with care; comic caricature with a documentary purpose; the large cast of a whole community; the essay and the sermon worked into the narrative; the problem play of ideas.
intellectual_concerns: Jewish immigration and the East End ghetto; assimilation and the loss of tradition; Zionism and the Jewish nation; poverty and sweated labour; the American melting pot; women's suffrage and the position of the Jewish woman.
historical_significance: Zangwill is the founding figure of English-Jewish literature: The Children of the Ghetto is the first major English book about the Jewish immigrant community, it made the East End ghetto a literary subject, and The Melting Pot gave the English language its most enduring metaphor for immigrant assimilation.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-English; the New Woman novel and the literature of marriage reform
literary_identity: Novelist and feminist; the writer who coined the phrase 'the New Woman' and the most influential woman novelist of the 1890s.
biography: Born Frances Elizabeth Bellenden Clarke at Donaghadee, County Down, on 10 June 1854, the daughter of a naval officer; she married a widowed army surgeon in 1870 and lived in India and Malta before settling in England in 1878. The Heavenly Twins (1893) made her famous and gave the 1890s the term 'New Woman'; she lectured for women's suffrage and against the Contagious Diseases Acts, became a Poor Law guardian in Tunbridge Wells, and died at Calne, Wiltshire, on 12 May 1943.
literary_profile: Grand wrote the New Woman novel as a weapon of social reform: her subject is the double standard, the sexual ignorance of girls and the marriage market, and her method is the long, argumentative, deliberately shocking novel that puts the case in the mouths of her heroines. The Heavenly Twins is the central English novel of the 1890s on marriage and sexual knowledge, and its popularity made the New Woman a national figure.
stylistic_characteristics: The long novel of debate with inserted documents, letters and essays; the comic satire of the marriage market; the shocking set-piece; the idealised New Woman heroine; direct address to the reader.
intellectual_concerns: The sexual double standard and marriage reform; girls' education and sexual knowledge; venereal disease and the Contagious Diseases Acts; the New Woman and her enemies; the position of women in the professions; mothering and child welfare.
historical_significance: Grand is the central English novelist of the New Woman and the coiner of the phrase that names her: The Heavenly Twins was the most discussed novel of 1893, it made the marriage question a national debate, and Grand's work is the founding text of the English novel of female sexual education.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the feminist essay and the New Woman novel
literary_identity: Novelist and essayist; the author of 'Marriage', the essay that provoked the greatest debate on marriage in Victorian England.
biography: Born Alice Mona Alison at Ryde, Isle of Wight, on 24 May 1854; she married James Henry Caird in 1877 and published her first novel, Whom Nature Leadeth, in 1883. Her essay 'Marriage' appeared in the Westminster Review in 1888 and provoked over 27,000 replies in the periodical press; she wrote seven novels, including The Daughters of Danaus (1894), and campaigned for women's suffrage and against vivisection. She died at Rye, Sussex, on 4 February 1932.
literary_profile: Caird wrote the most radical English feminist argument of the 1880s: 'Marriage' attacks the indissoluble marriage as a form of legalised slavery and calls for divorce on the grounds of incompatibility, and the storm it caused made the marriage question unavoidable. Her novels — especially The Daughters of Danaus — are the most intellectually ambitious of the New Woman fictions, and they test the feminist case against the actual lives of women.
stylistic_characteristics: The polemical essay with a plain and logical argument; the thesis novel with a wide social canvas; the analysis of the marriage law; the satirical portrait of the anti-feminist; the tragic ending refused by the conventional novel.
intellectual_concerns: Marriage and divorce law; the woman artist and the sacrifice of vocation; maternity and the 'maternal instinct'; the economic position of the married woman; the double standard; the ethics of heredity and vivisection.
historical_significance: Caird is the most radical English feminist theorist of the 1880s and the author of the essay that created the Victorian marriage debate: 'Marriage' is a founding document of English feminism, and The Daughters of Danaus is one of the most important New Woman novels.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the silver-fork novel, the historical romance and the domestic drama
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and politician; the most popular and most versatile English writer of the 1830s-40s, and the inventor of the 'silver-fork' fashion novel.
biography: Born Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer at London on 25 May 1803, the son of a general; he published Falkland in 1828 and Pelham in 1828, made his name as a dandy novelist, sat in Parliament from 1831 and became a baronet in 1838, taking the name Bulwer-Lytton. He wrote historical romances (The Last Days of Pompeii, 1834; Rienzi, 1835; Harold, 1848), the occult romance Zanoni (1842), and the domestic drama The Lady of Lyons (1838), and served as Secretary for the Colonies in 1858-59. He died at Torquay on 18 January 1873.
literary_profile: Bulwer-Lytton was the dominant popular novelist of the 1830s: he invented the 'silver-fork' novel of fashionable life in Pelham, established the English historical romance of classical antiquity in The Last Days of Pompeii, founded the occult romance in Zanoni, and wrote the theatre's most durable domestic drama. He was the first English novelist to unite society comedy, historical scholarship, the criminal underworld and the occult in a single prolific career, and Dickens called him the most popular writer of the age.
stylistic_characteristics: Fluent, epigrammatic society dialogue; the detailed description of dress, furniture and fashionable interiors; the historical set piece reconstructed from antiquarian reading; the sensational plot with a criminal secret; the rhetorical blank-verse declamation of the stage.
intellectual_concerns: Fashionable society and the pursuit of distinction; ambition, crime and the criminal underworld; the ancient world and its destruction; the occult and the will; politics and the reform of society; the artist and the adventurer.
historical_significance: Bulwer-Lytton is the missing link between Scott and Dickens: he created the fashionable novel, the classical historical romance and the occult novel, he wrote The Lady of Lyons, one of the most performed Victorian plays, and his influence on Dickens, Disraeli, Collins and the sensation novelists is direct. He is also, through the annual Bulwer-Lytton Fiction Contest, the most mocked novelist in English — a reputation that has obscured a genuinely inventive career.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the political novel and the romance of Young England
literary_identity: Novelist and statesman; the creator of the English political novel and twice Prime Minister of Britain.
biography: Born Benjamin D'Israeli in London on 21 December 1804, the son of a Jewish man of letters who had his children baptised; he was articled to a solicitor but made his name with Vivian Grey (1826) and travelled in the Levant in 1830-31. He entered Parliament in 1837 after four defeats and led the Young England group in the 1840s, publishing Coningsby (1844), Sybil (1845) and Tancred (1847); he became Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1852 and Prime Minister in 1868 and again in 1874-80, and died at Hughenden on 19 April 1881.
literary_profile: Disraeli created the English political novel: his trilogy of the 1840s uses the forms of romance and society comedy to argue that the aristocracy must recover its duty to the people, and Sybil is the first English novel to give the industrial working class a central place. He is also the great stylist of English political prose — his epigrams, his orientalising descriptions and his biting satirical portraits made him the most quotable novelist of the age, and his novels are the key documents of the Young England imagination.
stylistic_characteristics: Epigrammatic dialogue and brilliant repartee; the satirical portrait of a real political world; the oriental and the exotic as counters in an argument about England; the romance plot with a concealed identity; the rhetorical set speech; the purple descriptive passage.
intellectual_concerns: The condition of England and the two nations; aristocracy, duty and the Young England ideal; political ambition and the machinery of party; race, religion and the Jewish question; the East and the English imagination; money and the purchase of power.
historical_significance: Disraeli is the founder of the English political novel and its greatest practitioner: the Young England trilogy is the central literary expression of Victorian Toryism, Sybil first brought the industrial poor into fiction as a national question, and his epigrammatic style shaped the political prose of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the drama of ideas and the preface of the playwright
literary_identity: Dramatist, critic and socialist; the greatest English-language playwright of the modern age and the reformer of the Victorian stage.
biography: Born in Dublin on 26 July 1856, the son of a drunken civil servant and a musical mother; he left school at fifteen, followed his mother to London in 1876, and spent nine years in poverty writing five unsuccessful novels. He became a music critic, then drama critic for the Saturday Review (1895-98), joined the Fabian Society in 1884, and published Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant in 1898. His plays — Mrs Warren's Profession, Arms and the Man, Candida, Man and Superman, Pygmalion, Saint Joan — made him the dominant dramatist of the century; he won the Nobel Prize in 1925 and died at Ayot St Lawrence on 2 November 1950.
literary_profile: Shaw reinvented the English stage: he replaced the well-made play with the drama of argument, put the discussion at the centre of the action, and wrote long, combative prefaces that made every play a pamphlet. His subject is the conflict of ideas — prostitution and capitalism, love and the Life Force, poverty and the Salvation Army, class and speech — and his method is the inversion of the sentimental expectation: the soldier is a coward, the hero is a fool, and the woman chooses the man who will be useful to her.
stylistic_characteristics: Extended dialectical argument as dramatic action; the reversal of romantic and stage conventions; brilliant, epigrammatic and unflagging dialogue; the Shavian preface; the comic unmasking of the respectable; a prose that is colloquial, precise and rhetorically explosive.
intellectual_concerns: Poverty, prostitution and the economics of vice; socialism, the Fabian Society and the reform of society; marriage, the New Woman and the relations of the sexes; class and the ownership of language; war, heroism and the illusions of patriotism; the Life Force and creative evolution.
historical_significance: Shaw is the central English-language dramatist of the twentieth century and the decisive reformer of the Victorian stage: his prefaces and his plays made the theatre a place of argument, he created the modern drama of ideas, and plays from Pygmalion to Saint Joan have entered the permanent repertoire of the world.
